newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany races against clock to save flood-hit dike.
newsitem.headline: Germany races against clock to save flood-hit dike.

text.p: Thousands of German soldiers and volunteers raced against the clock on Sunday, hoping to prop up a dike along the Oder River long enough for floods to recede.
"We believe we have the situation under control but it remains critical," said a spokesman for the Brandenburg state interior ministry.
More than 10,000 soldiers and thousands of aid workers, water rescue teams, volunteer firefighters and villagers have struggled for nearly two weeks to to keep dikes along the Oder from bursting.

Brandenburg officials were cautiously optimistic that they could hold back the floods as long as water levels fell, but made clear that the danger of a break in the dam would persist until water levels lowered one and a half metres (five feet).
The dikes were so sodden from weeks of rain-induced floods that the chances of the river falling to safe levels before they burst remained small, according to rescue officials.
Germany has escaped the worst of a month of flooding that has killed more than 100 people in Poland and the Czech Republic, but damage to homes, businesses and farms has been extensive.

Should the dike break, which officials still say is more likely than not, water would flood the Oderbruch basin, an area 17 km (11 miles) wide and 50 km (30 miles) long on east Germany's frontier with Poland, engulfing villages, farms and factories.

For over a week the German army has employed a new technique to dry out the sodden dikes. First divers laid a sheet of plastic six metres (40 feet) deep in the water and 100 metres (330 feet) long to prevent the water from seeping through the dike.
Then they placed a pipe along the 100-metre section of dike most vulnerable to breaking and began sucking water out of the drenched foundations of the dam.

Repair work started on a second line of dikes near Zollbruecke. Private builders delivered tonnes of gravel to build a five-metre wall as a second line of defence which officials hope will stop the flood should the main dike burst.
The last time a break in the dike flooded the Oderbruch region was in 1947 near Reitwein.
The region lies below the level of the river, which presses against twists and turns in the dike as the Oder runs north to the Baltic Sea.
The Oderbruch basin was created 250 years ago by Frederick the Great of Prussia by draining swamps and redirecting the route of the Oder, gaining a huge valley of arable land.
Around 15,000 people have been evacuated from the region since last week and thousands more were warned to be ready to leave their homes at a moment's notice.
